processing: Orthodox black tea from a Nilgiri estate, exported mainly in leaf grades such as GFOP, FOP, BOP-1 and SFTGFOP. Little is documented about its methods beyond the usual orthodox process.
harvest_season: Little is documented about this garden's own calendar; as with other Nilgiri estates, the cool winter months are generally the most valued.
appearance_dry: As with other orthodox Nilgiri blacks, dark twisted leaf; the finer grades are the ones to look at closely.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Nilgiri black tea, a clear, bright amber-copper.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf, as is usual for Nilgiri black tea.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this garden's cup in particular. Nilgiri blacks in general are bright, brisk and lightly fruity rather than heavy.

brewing.notes: Western-style, as is usual for Nilgiri black tea. Pull it early if it starts to turn sharp.

vintage_note: As with other Nilgiri blacks, buy by season rather than by age and drink within a year or two of picking. Most of the crop goes abroad, so it may reach shops under an importer's lot name rather than as a branded estate tea.
description:
Havukal is a tea garden near Kotagiri in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu, one of the small group of southern estates noted for producing specialty lots. Its reputation rests on productivity and export more than on fame among home drinkers.

Most of its tea leaves India in grades such as GFOP, FOP, BOP-1 and SFTGFOP, with buyers mainly in Germany, Switzerland and the United States.

Little is written about how this garden's tea tastes on its own terms. Expect what is typical of the Nilgiris: a bright, brisk cup with some fruit and flowers, better brewed for three or four minutes than stewed.

When buying, ask for the grade and the picking month, since those tell you more than the estate name alone.
history: Little is documented about the garden's early years. The Thangavelu family bought Havukal in 1957 and has run it since, according to a trade press profile, which also credits it with an average of 4,031 kg of finished tea per hectare per year since 2009, among the highest in South India by some measures. About 85 percent of production is exported.
